referenced_fragment_samples.description:
Legal document. Court record. In the hand of Ḥalfon b. Menashshe. Location: Fustat. Dated: 1134. Abū Sa‘d and Abū Sahl form a partnership lasting 6.5 months to manufacture and sell glass. Half the capital (20 dinars in total) invested by Abū Sa‘d is considered a loan to Abū Sahl, who pledges title to his home as a security. This may suggest diversion from the commenda model, where the active partner is not liable for loss. But the partnership also diverges from the ‘eseq model, wherein only the active partner transacts. Both the profit/loss characteristics and the working arrangement between the partners suggests a craft partnership.

Abū Sa‘d is likely the senior partner: he is identified as al-Zajjāj, “the glazier” (i.e., a known personage in the field), while Abū Sahl is given no professional designation; as well, Abū Sa‘d invests all of the capital, suggesting that he may be short of liquid assets). Finally, the partnership stipulates that Abū Sa‘d need only work two shifts a week (suggesting he may have other business elsewhere), while Abū Sahl will work the rest of the week. 

Maṣliaḥ ha-Kohen, mentioned in line 54, functioned as leader of the Jewish community of Fusṭāṭ from 1127 to 1139. 

The signatories to the document, Natan b. Shelomo ha-Kohen and Natan b. Avraham ha-Levi, signed 5 months after the agreement was initiated, for unknown reasons. (Information from Lieberman, "A Partnership Society", pp. 17-21)

works.title: Studia Islamica

referenced_fragment_samples.description: Letter from Salāma b. Mūsā of Sfax, in Mazar, Sicily, to his partner Yehuda b. Moshe b. Sughmār, in Fustat. In Judaeo-Arabic. The longest letter in the Geniza. Dating: Early 1060s according to Ben-Sasson, based on the military disruptions mentioned. 7 September 1064 according to Gil, based on his identification of the battle discussed as that between the Qā'id of Sfax and the Zīrid ruler Tamīm b. Muʿizz on that date. Many details about a wide variety of commodities are mentioned, as well as financial transactions. "In essence, this long letter had a single purpose: to convince Yehuda b. Sughmār, Salāma's partner, not to dissolve the relationship between them." Salāma in fact agrees to the dissolution of the formal partnership (ṣuḥba), "I got your letters this year, and you swore that you wanted to dissolve. I want this to happen even more than you do. If the partnership continues there will be discord. . . . Now we no longer feel as we used to, when we relied on each other" (v4–5, 30). Despite this, Salāma suggests other ways of continuing their relationship, including Yehuda's mentoring of Nissim, a new junior associate Salāma is sending to him, and Yehuda's sending Salāma some goods in agency. Jessica Goldberg, Trade and Institutions, pp. 296–99 ("Salāma b. Mūsā's Disastrous Year"). Salāma opens with his shock and dismay at the letters full of blame that he had received from Yehuda. "I had expected you to congratulate me on my survival in al-Mahdiyya, my deliverance from destruction, and the terrible ordeal (al-mawqif al-ʿaẓīm, also mentioned in r23) that I would not wish on anyone. I was bound (kutiftu) and almost killed (or executed, ʿuriḍtu ʿalā l-sayf) four times (or five—the ink is flaked here). Even if there were no partnership (sharika), love, (mawadda), or association (ṣuḥba) between us, this would have been incumbent on you. Now, more than one year later, the terror has not subsided, rather the fright remains in my heart. My greatest trial in al-Mahdiyya was my concern for your business. . . ." Interestingly, when Salāma mentions Yehuda's illnesses of last year (mā laḥaqak tilk al-sana min al-ḍuʿf wa-l-tawajjuʿ, r75), there is not a word of the usual sympathy or congratulations on his recovery. Gil understands Halper 414 to be a follow-up from this letter; Goldberg believes that Halper 414, a small sheet, was inserted into Halper 389, which seems to agree with Goitein, who calls it a "continuation" of Halper 389 (see Goitein notes linked to PGPID 35364). Information from Goldberg, Ben-Sasson, and Gil. ASE; MR

referenced_fragment_samples.description: Dialogue between the Misri (the man from Old Cairo) and the Rifi (the man from the countryside). Literary, probably late, very colloquial. The writer is consistent with diacritics, not replicated in this transcription. Full of interesting stereotypes and vocabulary of city versus country life: prices, foods, clothes, bathing habits, goods available in the market, sewage ("your bowel movements remain with you, their stench is blinding"). Also names Bayn al-Qasrayn and the glorious fruit and paper markets at Bab Zuwaylah. In the third and final leaf of the story (recto of BL OR 5565G.27), the Misri and the Rifi declare a truce. Then the narrator chimes in with a prayer and an announcement of who he is and how great his stories are, for the benefit of the gathered audience: "I am the מחסווך (??) the Jew... my name is Sulayman... my speech is well-balanced, my meanings divine... my trade in Misr is cantor, as a poet I am known in the Rif...." The verso of BL OR 5565G.27 then begins a comic tale about someone whose pack was seized by a greedy man; they go to court, and the judge says he will award it to whomever can say what's in the pack. ASE.

case.question: Can you tell me about Ketubah's in the Cairo Genizah?

must_include: Grounded, page-cited scholarship on Genizah ketubbot.
should_include: Specific ketubba shelf marks when named.

response.answer:
Scholars examining the ketubba (Jewish marriage contract) emphasize its origins in customary law and its subsequent legal crystallization. **Friedman**, p. 2: "The text of the ketubba (plural ketubbot), the Jewish marriage contract, is designated in Tannaitic sources as leshon hedyot, the language or formulary of laymen." By the late second Temple period and the early second century, its formula had begun to crystalize. **Friedman**, p. 2: "The Tannaim attached legal significance to its precise wording and formulation and based halakhic decisions on it."

While later medieval Diaspora contracts largely followed a standardized model, this uniformity has historically obscured regional variations. **Friedman**, p. 7: "But in the overwhelming majority of cases, the basic formulary essentially conforms with the Babylonian tradition of the ketubba..." However, the discovery of Palestinian-style ketubbot has challenged the assumption of a single, unchanging Babylonian formulary. The Cairo Genizah preserves important Palestinian-style marriage contracts, particularly from the end of the Gaonic period. **Friedman**, p. 9.

These Geniza documents provide crucial comparative material for understanding early proposal and acceptance clauses. Scholars analyzing these texts note specific linguistic variations in the second-person feminine singular pronoun used in proposal clauses, observing that certain restorations of the formula are doubtful due to grammatical inconsistencies.

The retrieved scholarship does not record specific shelf marks, dates, or scribes for the Geniza ketubbot, nor does it detail the full range of financial stipulations or conduct clauses found in these contracts. The available texts focus primarily on the historical development of the formulary, the distinction between Babylonian and Palestinian traditions, and the linguistic analysis of proposal and acceptance formulae.

bibliography_results.title: Jewish Marriage in Palestine: The Kettubba texts
bibliography_results.author: Mordechai Akiva Friedman
bibliography_results.description: This page introduces the primary sources for studying Palestinian ketubba traditions. It first discusses early fragmentary marriage contracts from Murabba'at (Judean Desert), written in Aramaic and Greek during the early Tannaitic period, noting their historical importance but also their limitations due to antiquity and poor preservation for later halakhic study. The main focus then shifts to the Cairo Geniza fragments, specifically Palestinian-style marriage contracts from the end of the Gaonic period. The author highlights that despite their fragmentary nature and damage, the large number of these Geniza documents (78 fragments from 65 ketubbot, including early Hebrew manuscripts on paper from Damascus, 933 CE) allows for in-depth comparative study and restoration of lacunae. The book is dedicated to analyzing and editing these Geniza texts, which have received limited scholarly attention despite being available for over eighty years.

also found in Murabba'at are written in Greek. The parties are Jewish, and

These documents, written in the early Tannaitic period, are indispensable
materials for the investigation of the history of Jewish marriage law and
the ketubba. As of the present, they have received only limited attention by
the scholarly community.
The importance of this find notwithstanding, the study of the Palestinian
ketubba traditions on the basis of these texts has distinct, inherent limita-
tions. Their very antiquity restricts them from serving as sources for the
study of the particular Palestinian traditions of the ketubba, since they
were written before the crystalization of the halakha during the Tannaitic
period; and, obviously, they cannot be expected to reflect the formulae and
stipulations which developed and took root in Eretz Israel during the
Amoraic period, during which time the separate centers of learning in
Palestine and Babylonia emerged and formulated their two Talmuds and
distinct traditions. More serious limitations for the study of these docu-
ments are the small number of contracts discovered and their poor state of
preservation. All are most fragmentary and are written in obscure scripts.
There are several gaps in their formulae; and even where the texts are in-
tact, their decipherment is often uncertain. References to these documents

pare these texts with the "traditional" (i.e., Babylonian) ketubba. The marriage docu-
ments from DJD, II, are reprinted with comments in Koffmahn, Doppelurkunden, pp.
114 ff. Babata's marriage contract: Y. Yadin, "Expedition D-The Cave of the Let-
ters," IEJ, XII (1962), 244–245. On p. 245, Yadin noted that the wording "usually

are made in almost every section of the present study, and several correc-
tions are suggested to doubtful readings in the edited texts.
The Geniza fragments.-This brings us to the second source of
materials: the Palestinian-style marriage contracts written towards the end
of the Gaonic period which were preserved in the Cairo Geniza. Also most
of these documents are in most fragmentary pieces. Many are written in
scripts that are difficult to decipher and have suffered various degrees of
damage by water and other natural forces as well as intentional mutiliza-
tion and the ravages of man. 18 But they have been preserved in a large
enough number to make possible a comparative study in depth, on a broad
basis, in which most of these difficulties can be overcome and almost all of
the hiatuses restored. The present book is devoted to an analysis of these
Palestinian ketubba fragments and to editions of their texts.
Seventy-eight Geniza fragments, from ten separate libraries and belong-
ing to sixty-five ketubbot have been assembled by this writer. The docu-
ments range in size from large self-containing pieces to small scraps. Most
are written on parchment; but a few, particularly formularies and copies,
are on paper. These include what may be the earliest known Hebrew
manuscripts on Oriental paper, from Damascus, 933 (nos. 53-55).19 Six
contracts have been pieced together from two or more fragments, one from
four pieces now housed in three libraries. 20 More than eighty years have
passed since the "discovery” of the Geniza and the removal of its contents,
in stages, to various libraries and museums in Europe and America.
Although these documents have been available to three generations of
scholars, they have received relatively little attention. This has been the

for other purposes as well.

copy within another document), 53-55 (leaves of a court book), 57 (leaf of a court
book). On early Hebrew manuscripts on paper, see M. Beit-Arié, Hebrew Codicology
(Paris, 1976), pp. 20–21.

Title: Jewish Marriage in Palestine: The Kettubba texts
Authors: Mordechai Akiva Friedman
Subjects: Ketubah, Jewish marriage, Palestine, Cairo Genizah, Marriage contracts, Jewish law, Geniza studies
Summary: This page discusses the historical understanding of Jewish marriage contracts (ketubbot), particularly the long-held assumption of a uniform Babylonian formulary that remained unchanged for centuries. It critiques this view, citing scholars like L.M. Epstein, and highlights how recent discoveries of Palestinian-style ketubbot, including those from the Judean Desert (pre-Bar Kokhba revolt), have challenged this notion by revealing distinct traditions of formulation.
Main text: INTRODUCTION
i A
¡ A
AN OVERVIEW
7
kitchenware. Similarly, these fragments include various types of special
stipulations dealing with the conduct of the groom and bride and their
obligations, according to the parties' status and special needs.
These documents differ in the text of the formulary of the ketubba as
well. But in the overwhelming majority of cases, the basic formulary essen-
tially conforms with the Babylonian tradition of the ketubba, known
primarily from the formularies of the Babylonian Geonim and from cità-
tions in their responsa (and subsequently from the formularies of medieval
authorities). The same is true concerning the marriage contracts of the dif-
ferent communities of the Jewish Diaspora from the Middle Ages until
modern times. They contain minor, yet interesting variations. But, with few
exceptions (discussed below), all of them are loyal to the ketubba tradition
of the Babylonian Geonim.
The Babylonian-style ketubba and students of the Jewish marriage con-
tract.-The basic similarity between the ketubba traditions of various
Jewish communities, known from conventional sources, and the Babylo-
nian formulary has misled students of the marriage contract for centuries.
Scholars, who were acquainted with only this ketubba tradition, assumed
that the basic formulary of this text had been in-use already in Mishnaic
and Talmudic times. Since then, through modern times, it was used ex-
clusively by all Jewish communities and underwent only inconsequential
additions and revisions. Theories and conclusions as to the development of
the marriage contract, its significance and the laws and institutions as-
sociated with it, were based on these assumptions. Mordekhai b. Hillel
(Germany, thirteenth century) imagined that the phrase "the best and most
choice of my properties," written in the pledging clause in the ketubba,
could have been introduced by Simeon b. Sheṭaḥ (first century B.C.E).14
Statements by L.M. Epstein in his important work, The Jewish Mar-
riage Contract (appeared in 1927, some thirty years after the “discovery”
of the Geniza).-the only book-length study of the ketubba written to
date-are typical of this approach. For example, of the proposal fòrmula
"Be to me a wife according to the law of Moses and Israel," Epstein wrote
14 At the end of his code-commentary to Ketubbot. See the discussion below, ch. vi ất n.
42.
"
that "for almost two thousand years, Jews have employed this formula for
their ketubot without the slightest change, even as it feads in our ketubah
today." 15 As recently as 1968, in the introduction to a handsome volume
dealing with illuminated kétubbot, we read that since the time of Simeon b.
Sheṭaḥ "the Aramaic text has remained in use to this day, unchanged in
any detail." 16
Discovery of fragments of Palestinian ketubbot.-We now know that this
presumption of a unilateral, vertical continuity of formulation does not
reflect historical realities, neither for the phrase "the best and most choice
of my properties," nor for the proposal formula, nor, for that matter, for
the general formula of the ketubba. The recent discoveries of fragments of
Palestinian-style ketubbot have opened new vistas for the study of Jewish
marriage contracts and have revealed traditions of formulating the ketubba
distinct from that of the Babylonian Geonim.
Fragments from the Judean Desert.-The new materials come from two
separate finds. The first consists of three fragmentary Aramaic Jewish
marriage contracts from the Judean Desert, from the years preceding the
Bar Kokhba revolt, in the early second century C.E. Two of these have
been published (in DJD, II, appeared in 1961); and the third, Babata's
ketubba, discovered by Yadin in the "Cave of Letters," has been described,
with brief citations, in a preliminary report and, at the time of this writing,
15 Epstein, JMC, p. 57. (See the discussion below at the beginning of ch. iii B, 1.)' This
basic attitude crops up throughout Epstein's book, and the failure to make adequate
use of available* Geniza materials is the book's most fundamental methodological
shortcoming.
The prejudice in favor of the uniform Babylonian ketubba tradition appears in most
studies dealing with aspects of the marriage contract, and there is hardly a point in
cataloguing these. See, e.g., ch. iii B, nn. 62, 79; iv A at n. 18; et passim. Cf. E.Y.
'Kutscher, "The Language of the 'Genesis Apocryphon,' A Preliminary Study," in
Scripta Hierosolymitana, IV (Jerusalem, 1957), p. 32, who compared a phrase in the
Genesis Apocryphon with one in "the Jewish Marriage Contract," i.e., the (Gaonic)
Babýlonian ketubba. Cf. ch. i B, n. 17.
16 D. Davidovitch, The Ketuba: Jewish Marriage Contracts through the Ages (Hebrew
title, Ha-Ketubba be-‘Iṭṭurim, “The Illuminated Ketubba”) (Tel Aviv, 1968), p. 113 (p.
8 in Hebrew).

Summary: The page discusses the views of Benjamin, a learned Jew, and his interpretations of biblical texts and Talmudic law, including his dualist beliefs and connection to the Karaite movement. It also references the influence of Islamic dualism on Karaite thought, the relationship between Karaites and the Zandiks (Zadokites), and the origins of the term 'Karaite' derived from the Torah. The text mentions scholars like al-Sa'udi, Geyer, and Poznanski in the context of Karaite studies.
Main text: הקראים
[סעיפים 160–163]
אלעכְּבַּרִי. היה אדם מלומד, בקי במקרא ובדברי הרבניים, ונאמר עליו שבמשך שנים רבות
היה דיין. הוא נקט דרך אמצעית בין הכתובים ובין ה'קיאס' (ההיקש, האנלוגיה), ובמילים
אחרות: השתדל לשמור אמונים גם לכתוב כפשוטו. קִרְקְסאני מונה את השקפותיו של
בנימין: (א) אלוהים ברא מלאך והוא שעסק בכל ענייני הבריאה, הוא השולח את השליחים
והמראה את המופתים ומחדש כל דבר בעולם. (ב) ענייני ייבום: אין האשה הנשואה חייבת
בייבום, אלא רק הארוסה. (ג) "והיה הבן הבכר לשניאה' (דב' כא: טו), פירש שבן השנואה
הוא שייחשב תמיד הבכור, אף אם יהיה צעיר מבן האחרת. (ד) 'אם במחתרת ימצא הגנב'
(שמ' כב: א), אפילו חפירה שהיתה שם לפני כן, ואפילו חורבה. (ה) 'לא תסגיר עבד' (דב'
כג: טז), אפילו היה אדוניו מישראל. (ו) אסר שיינשאו איש ואשה שהיתה להם מינקת
משותפת. (ז) הילד חייב במצוות משהתחיל לדבר. (ח) תשרי וניסן ייקבעו ראשיהם על פי
הראייה, החודשים האחרים על פי חשבון. (ט) לגבי עופות התיר גם שחיטה גם מליקה.
(י) שלל עונש מוות לארוסה ששכב עמה אדם במדבר, אפילו הסכימה. (יא) שלל את טומאת
הנפל; רק המת באוויר העולם מטמא. (יב) רק קבר שהוא בחוץ מטמא, לא אם הוא בתוך
הבית. (יג) אם בעל אדם את הנידה, בגדיה מטמאים וירחץ את בגדיו ואת גופו; אם היתה
לבושה בבגדיה, אינם מטמאים את בגדיו וירחץ רק את גופו. (יד) אין האדם מקבל טומאה
בשעת בין הערביים.
ניכר שקִרְקַסאני הביא את השקפות בנימין באופן רדוד ופשטני, והרבה בפרטים טפלים
(ולעתים תמוהים). הד מזה נקלט אצל הסופר הערבי אלסעודי, הכותב על כת יהודית
שנקראת 'אלבנימינייה', הם חסידי בנימין, המאמינים באחדות האל, אך סבורים שיש לו
יריב בקרב ברואיו הפועל נגדו, והרע ממנו יבוא ולא מן האל. ניכר שבנימין הביא עמו
שרידים של מסורת דואליסטית שאי אפשר להגדיר בוודאות את שורשיה. מאן סבר שפעלו
עליו השפעות אִסְמַעיליות, ואמנם האִסְמַעילים קלטו רעיונות דואליסטיים, וגם את הרעיון
של הבריאה העקיפה. הרעיון של התייחסות הקראים על הצדוקים, שהיו הדואליסטים
המובהקים לפי כמה מקורות ערביים, תרם לדעה בדבר הדואליזם של הקראים. הצדוקים
נקראו 'זִנְדיקים' ('זָנָאדְקה'; זִנְדיקים פירושו בדרך כלל מאניכאים, אבל גם דואליסטים
באופן כללי). חוקרים מודרניים, שטרם הכירו את כתבי מדבר יהודה, אמנם ייחסו לקראים
(החל מבנימין) קשר עם הצדוקים הקדומים; לדברי גייגר המשיכו דעות הצדוקים להתקיים
אצל הקראים ודברים דומים כתבו גם הרכבי
אצל השומרונים תחילה, ואחר כך
ופוזננסקי. ואולם אין יסוד של ממש להשקפה בדבר קשר, במישרין או בעקיפין, בין
הצדוקים הקדמונים ובין הקראים.
בנימין הנהאונדי היה כנראה הראשון שהשתמש בשם 'בני מקרא', והיה זה אצלו שם
כולל לאנשי הכיתות, וניכר שעל פי תפיסת קראים ראשונים אלה, ובניגוד לסברות שהובעו
במחקר המודרני (כגון שהשם קראים הושפע מה'דאעי' הערבי), השם קראים אמנם נגזר מן
המקרא. נראה שבנימין הוא שהשיג את ההתחברות עם בית ענן וסיעתו; אולי בזכות היותו
-

לבושה בבגדיה, אינם מטמאים את בגדיו וירחץ רק את גופו. (יד) אין האדם מקבל טומאה
בשעת בין הערביים.
ניכר שקִרְקַסאני הביא את השקפות בנימין באופן רדוד ופשטני, והרבה בפרטים טפלים
(ולעתים תמוהים). הד מזה נקלט אצל הסופר הערבי אלסעודי, הכותב על כת יהודית
שנקראת 'אלבנימינייה', הם חסידי בנימין, המאמינים באחדות האל, אך סבורים שיש לו
יריב בקרב ברואיו הפועל נגדו, והרע ממנו יבוא ולא מן האל. ניכר שבנימין הביא עמו
שרידים של מסורת דואליסטית שאי אפשר להגדיר בוודאות את שורשיה. מאן סבר שפעלו
עליו השפעות אִסְמַעיליות, ואמנם האִסְמַעילים קלטו רעיונות דואליסטיים, וגם את הרעיון
של הבריאה העקיפה. הרעיון של התייחסות הקראים על הצדוקים, שהיו הדואליסטים
המובהקים לפי כמה מקורות ערביים, תרם לדעה בדבר הדואליזם של הקראים. הצדוקים
נקראו 'זִנְדיקים' ('זָנָאדְקה'; זִנְדיקים פירושו בדרך כלל מאניכאים, אבל גם דואליסטים
באופן כללי). חוקרים מודרניים, שטרם הכירו את כתבי מדבר יהודה, אמנם ייחסו לקראים
(החל מבנימין) קשר עם הצדוקים הקדומים; לדברי גייגר המשיכו דעות הצדוקים להתקיים
אצל הקראים ודברים דומים כתבו גם הרכבי
אצל השומרונים תחילה, ואחר כך
ופוזננסקי. ואולם אין יסוד של ממש להשקפה בדבר קשר, במישרין או בעקיפין, בין
הצדוקים הקדמונים ובין הקראים.
בנימין הנהאונדי היה כנראה הראשון שהשתמש בשם 'בני מקרא', והיה זה אצלו שם
כולל לאנשי הכיתות, וניכר שעל פי תפיסת קראים ראשונים אלה, ובניגוד לסברות שהובעו
במחקר המודרני (כגון שהשם קראים הושפע מה'דאעי' הערבי), השם קראים אמנם נגזר מן
המקרא. נראה שבנימין הוא שהשיג את ההתחברות עם בית ענן וסיעתו; אולי בזכות היותו

bibliography_results.description: This page discusses the historical and legal development of the Jewish marriage contract (ketubba). It explains how Tannaitic sages derived legal principles from interpreting the ketubba's language, which was considered 'leshon hedyot' (language of laymen). The text details how the ketubba's formula crystallized by the second century and how Tannaim attached legal significance to its wording, adding to and emending it. Hai Gaon's explanation of 'interpreting laymen's formulary' is provided. The page also covers the ketubba's continued role as a source of law in Amoraic and post-Talmudic periods. INTRODUCTION

i A

Passages from Tannaitic sources show that R. Eleazar b.
Azariaḥ, R. Judah, R. Yose, and other sages similarly derived legal princi-
ples from interpreting the language of the marriage contract.³
The text of the ketubba (plural ketubbot), the Jewish marriage contract,
is designated in Tannaitic sources as leshon hedyot, the language or for-
mulary of laymen.4 It primarily developed, in the customary law, on the
basis of free contract and was given its form by the professional scribes. By
the late second Temple period and the early second century, its formula
had begun to crystalize. The Tannaim attached legal significance to its
precise wording and formulation and based halakhic decisions on it. They
also added to the formulary and emended it.' The process of "interpreting
laymen's formulary" (dorshin leshon hedyot) is explained in an il-
luminating comment by Hai Gaon: "They examined in detail the language
which laymen wrote in their documents and interpreted it in the same way,

BT B.M. 104b. See the discussion below in ch. ii C, at nn. 15 ff., concerning how the
regulations for a married couple's place of residence were derived from interpreting
their marriage contract.

AN OVERVIEW
3
that they examined in detail and interpreted the words of the Torah, not by
the simple meaning but by other interpretations."6
The text of the marriage contract continued to serve as a source of law
in the Amoraic and post-Talmudic periods. Yet,, while it is axiomatic that
the ketubba is perhaps the most important document for the study of
Jewish marriage and family law, and the changing status of women
throughout the ages, a complete formulary of this writ is not preserved-in
the Talmud.
Uniformity of ketubbot and the Babylonian tradition.-Over the past
several centuries there has been an increasing tendency, in almost all
Jewish communities, to write the ketubba according to a brief, largely
stereotyped formula, including the sums-given for marriage payments and
dowry. The formula was considered to be essentially fixed, and little
latitude was permitted for digressions. Excessive divergencies were as-
sociated with sectarianism. An early manifestation of this attitude may be
cited from a query addressed to the Gaon Natronai (about 720). Among
the religious offences of the followers of the false Messiah Severus, listed in
the query, was the fact that "they do not write marriage contracts in the
form prescribed by our sages.” Natronai decried the "spoilage of marriage
the word ketubba שמעון בן שטח תיקן כתובה לאשה (166 In BT Shabbat 145 (and .(2
probably refers to the "(delayed) mohar payment" and not to the "marriage contract.”
(For this meaning of ketubba, see ch. iv A, mr. 5. Note, e.g., Enc. Jud., XIV, 1564: “Ac-
cording to one tradition, he was responsible for the institution of the written ketubbah,
[the marriage contract]……..” S. Tal, Sinai, XXXVI, 188: “According to the concep-
tion of the PT [MAF: 'ketubba is from the Torah'], since the time the Torah was given
it was the practice to write a marriage contract." Cf. S. Y. Cohen in Mazkeret ……
Ý. I.
ha-Levi Herzog [Jerusalem, 1962], p. 546, n. 7 and esp. pp. 547-8.) See Lieberman,
Tosefta Ki-Fshutah, VI, 369, for the meaning of 'n in this passage. Cf. E. Neufeld,
Ancient Hebrew Marriage Laws (London, 1944), p. 158. For emendations of the
ketubba by the Tannaim, see, for example, the discussion of Rabbi Nathan and Rabbi
Judah ha-Nasi on the text of the benin dikhrin stipulation to be fixed in the Mishnah:
PT Ket. IV.12, 29a; PT B.B. VIII.6, 16b; BT B:B. 131a:
6
7
Quoted by Ramban (Naḥmanides) in his commentary to B.M. 104a (and in Shița Me-
qubbeşet a.l.) and by Zachariah b. Judah Aghmātī, Digest to B.M., p. 143. Cf. the
other commentaries to B.M. 104a and esp. Shița Mequbbeṣet. Hai's comment seems
to imply that hedyoṬ means “layman" in contrast with the sages. This point is express-
ly made by most of the commentaries; cf., e.g., Rashi and Tosafot to B.M. 104a. This
contrasts with Zachariah Aghmāti's interpretation (Digest, p. 143, according to the
marginal note there, in the name of R. Hai!), viz. that hedyoț here means “human.”
(Cf. ch. v C, Appendix I.) See Lieberman, Tosefta Ki-Fshuțah, VĮ, 245-246; cf. M.
Elon, Jewish Law (Hebrew; Jerusalem, 1973), II, 350 ff. See BT Yev. 117a, “Rav
Ḥisda said, ‘……. They expounded the text of the ketubba. Should we not expound the
text of the Torah?”” Cf. below n. 30.
Amoraic: Cf., e.g., concerning the divorce provision, PT Ket. VII.7, 31c; several ex-
amples in PT Ket. IV. 11-14, 29a-b and BT Ket. 51 ff. deal with interpretations of the
authorized texts of ketubba formulae found in the Mishnah and baraitot. Cf. ch. v G,
n. 9. For an interesting example from the post-Talmudic period for the basing of
marital obligations on a ketubba formula not cited in the Talmud, see the discussion in
ch. iii B, 1c (following n. 70).

bibliography_results.title: Jewish Marriage in Palestine: The Kettubba texts
bibliography_results.author: Mordechai Akiva Friedman
bibliography_results.description: This page analyzes proposal and acceptance formulae in Jewish marriage contracts (ketubbot), comparing texts from the Judean Desert (DJD II, no. 20 and no. 21) with later Palestinian Geniza documents. It discusses the linguistic forms of proposal, such as 'תהוא לי לאנתה כדין מנושה]' and 'לאנת[ ... ]ן מושה ויהודאי' from Babata's ketubba, suggesting alternative restorations. The text also highlights the emphasis on procreation in Palestinian marriage deeds, noting phrases like 'the mother of children' (אמהון דבנין) found in various documents, indicating it was a standard formula.

The text also highlights the emphasis on procreation in Palestinian marriage deeds, noting phrases like 'the mother of children' (אמהון דבנין) found in various documents, indicating it was a standard formula.

The proposal formulae of the Palestinian ketubbot from the Geniza and

us in reading and restoring the fragmentary marriage contracts from the

Both the restoration הואי לי לאנתו or הרי את לי לאנתו proposal formulae
and the interpretation of the line as a direct proposal, based on the com-
parison to the formulae from the Talmud and the later ketubba, are doubt-
ful. First of all, the form for the sec. pers. fem. personal pronoun is unlikely
to have been 'nx, but, rather, nx (as, for example, in DJD, II, no. 21:12, in
the following text, which is also a marriage contract) or лx. Furthermore,
were a direct proposal intended, one would expect the imperative "17 (or

of the Palestinian marriage deeds, expressions which may be seen as
reflecting the goals and motives ascribed to marriage within the tradition.
On the basis of the most conspicuous of these phrases one is led to con-
clude that the primary goal of marriage was procreation. Two documents,
nos. 27:6 and 56:5, both from Damascus and written by the same scribe,
have the bride asked to become not only the groom's wife but also
"127 "the mother of children." The identical formula is transposed to the
bride's acceptance or to the affirmation of the conclusion of the marriage
in three other documents: no. 8b:9-10, a formulary; no. 12:7, written by
she" והוות ליה לאנתו ולאמהון דבנין :the Palestinian Gaon Elijah at Ramle
became wife to him and the mother of children"; and no. 59:13 from Tyre,
in Hebrew, " or³) nwx³ num². No. 8c:7-8 repeats the expression a sec-
and he acquired her as wife and the" וזכה בה לאנתו ולאמהון דבנין :ond time
mother of children." The occurrence of the expression in several docu-
ments, from different locations, including a formulary, demonstrates that it
was a standard phrase of the Palestinian-style ketubba and did not reflect
any peculiar circumstances of the specific marriages, such as the groom
having children from a previous marriage. Special stipulations to care for
the children of a spouse from a former marriage are found in many Geniza
ketubbot but not as part of the proposal or acceptance formulae. 33 A
similar emphasis on this aspect of the wife's role in marriage appears in the
formulary of Samaritan marriage contracts, where the wife is compared to
"Eve, created from man's rib, to be a helper and for procreation."34
32 Y. Yadin, IEJ, XII (1962), 245.
33 See Goitein, Education, pp. 29-31. Additional examples may now be added.
34 See M. Gaster, “Die Ketubbah bei den Samaritanern," MGWJ, LIV (1910), 185 et
passim. Cf. V.A. Tcherikover, A. Fuks, M. Stern, Corpus Papyrorum Judaicarum, III
(Cambr., Mass., 1964), no. 513, pp. 102-104, a Greek deed of divorce between
Samaritans, dated 586, “... whereas we were recently united with one another with a
view to lawful matrimony and community of life and for the procreation of children,
according to the custom of men, with fair hopes...."

Main text: [סעיפים 142–143]
בבל ומחלוקת הלוח
ראינו שבאותו מכתב מן החצי הראשון של המאה התשיעית סומך ראש הגולה את עיקר
טענתו על הכלל לא אד"ו ראש'. במאמר שפרסם בתש"ם ביקש מ"ד הר להוכיח, שאת
הכלל המונע את תחולת ראש השנה ביום א' הוסיפו לכללי הלוח העברי מאוחר יחסית,
במאה השביעית לספירה בקירוב. ואולם היעדרו של כלל בסיסי כל כך עשוי היה לגרום
שינוי גדול בפרטי התאריכים; והנה דווקא מן המאה השביעית, מתחילתה, יש לנו מידע על
תאריכים מקבילים לפי שלושת הלוחות: היהודי, הנוצרי והמוסלמי. לפי אחת המסורות
המוסלמיות הקדומות חל בואו של מַחֲמַד לאלמדינה ביום ב', 12 ברַבִּיע א ; אבל 12 ברַבִּיע
א חל ביום ו', ונראה שאותה מסורת נגעה לבואו לקבא, מעין פרוור של אלמדינה שהיה
מאוכלס יהודים, והיה זה ב־8 ברַבִּיע א; יום ב', 8 ברַבִּיע א בשנה הראשונה להגירה חל
ב־20 בספטמבר 622; לדברי המסורת המוסלמית מצא אז מַחֲמַד את היהודים צמים, כי היה
זה יום העאשורא שלהם, כלומר היום העשירי בחודש הראשון, שהוא, כמובן, יום
הכיפורים. ואמנם, לפי הטבלאות, חל יום הכיפורים באותה שנה ב־20 בספטמבר, וראש
השנה חל אז כמובן בשבת. אני חולק על הנתונים שמביא מ"ד הֶר במאמרו המעניין. הוא
מפרש פסקה ב'מעשים לבני ארץ ישראלי כאילו נאמר בה שרשאים להתיר נדרים בליל ראש
השנה שחל במוצאי שבת, ומכאן ראיה שראש השנה יכול לחול ביום א', בניגוד ל'לא אד"ו
ראש'. אבל באמת נאמר שם: "אין מתירין נדרין בלילי ראש השנה בשבת; ובמוצאי השבת
מותר'. אין לי ספק שהכוונה היא שרשאים להתיר את הנדר רק בתום היום, לעת מוצאי
השבת, ומשמעות השבת כאן: המועד (כלומר במוצאי ראש השנה), והוא פשוטה של פסקה
זו. בהמשך מבקש הֶר לקבוע את זמן כתיבתם של הקטעים מספרות המעשים' על ידי
מציאת הזמן שבו החליטו לדעתו למנוע שראש השנה יחול ביום א', כלומר להוסיף את האי
ל׳לא דו ראשי. לשם כך הוא מסתמך על שלושה מקורות: (א) כתובת קבורה מצוער משנת
דירס"ג (503 לספירה) של אשה שמתה ביום ג' שהיה י"א באלול (וראש השנה שאחריו חל
אם כן ביום א'); (ב) פסקה באיגרת שרירא גאון האומרת שאחאי בן הונא מת ביום א', ד'
באדר (ושוב נמצא ראש השנה חל ביום א'; לפי הטבלאות של מאהלר חל אז ד׳ באדר ביום
ב׳; וראה לעיל, סעיף 86); (ג) דברי רב אחאי בשאילתות, פרשת ויקהל, לפורים, על זמנם
של חכמים הראשונים שהיו בקיאין בחשבון מולד לבנה ובדיקדוקי סוד העיבור; היה יום
ערבה בא בשבת, ופורים בשבת, ומקרא מגלה בשבת, ומוציאין לולב בשבת, ותוקעין שופר
בשבת שחל ראש השנה להיות בו; אבל היום, שאין חכמים בקיאין בחשבון תולדות לבנה
ובדיקדוקי סוד העיבור, גזרו חכמים' וכו'. כאן מוצא הֶר הוכחה שעד סמוך לזמנו של רב
אחאי, כלומר לחצי הראשון של המאה השמינית, עדיין חל ראש השנה לפעמים ביום א'
(שיום הערבה היה בא בשבת'), ורק באותו זמן גזרו חכמים למנוע אפשרות זו. אבל יש
לשים לב שלפי אותה פסקה לא רק יום א' נעדר מ'לא אדו', אלא אף יום ד' (׳פורים בשבת',
שאז יחול ראש השנה ביום ד'). אין ספק שנוסח זה של השאילתות אין בו היגיון והוא
משובש; אף אין ללמוד מלשונו ׳היום.... גזרו חכמים׳ (אם אמנם כך התבטא רב אחאי), על
221

bibliography_results.title: Jewish Marriage in Palestine: The Kettubba texts

bibliography_results.description: This page analyzes the historical development and significance of different stylistic formulations in Jewish marriage contracts (ketubbot), particularly contrasting the ancient Palestinian 'subjective' style (where the groom directly declares) with the later Babylonian 'objective' style ('he said'). It suggests the subjective style, found in a large group of Palestinian ketubbot from the Genizah, may represent an older form with a 'covenanting character' or a function similar to a writ of qiddushin. The text also discusses the likely late development of the objective style in Babylonia and its subsequent influence on later Palestinian ketubbot, noting instances where scribes combined these styles.

Title: Jewish Marriage in Palestine: The Kettubba texts
Authors: Mordechai Akiva Friedman
Subjects: Ketubah, Jewish marriage, Palestine, Cairo Genizah, Marriage contracts, Jewish law, Geniza studies
Summary: This page analyzes the historical development and significance of different stylistic formulations in Jewish marriage contracts (ketubbot), particularly contrasting the ancient Palestinian 'subjective' style (where the groom directly declares) with the later Babylonian 'objective' style ('he said'). It suggests the subjective style, found in a large group of Palestinian ketubbot from the Genizah, may represent an older form with a 'covenanting character' or a function similar to a writ of qiddushin. The text also discusses the likely late development of the objective style in Babylonia and its subsequent influence on later Palestinian ketubbot, noting instances where scribes combined these styles.
Main text: 128
SETTING THE SCENE
ii D
ii D
FORMULATION
129
The ancient (Palestinian) ketubba style, now identified from the quote in
the Tosefta and PT, thus survived in the largest group (A) of Palestinian
marriage contracts from the Geniza. The possible theoretical significance
of this style, with the direct subjective declaration of the groom, for an un-
derstanding of the (original?) function and nature of the ketubba is a com-
plex, speculative matter that we shall not consider in depth here. But we do
note that the subjective opening suits a private deed and also a document
of the "dispositive" category, i.e., a deed which itself effects a change in
legal status, similar to the get. 25 L.M. Epstein commented on the style of
the later (Babylonian-type) ketubba as contrasted with quotes from the
marriage contract in Talmudic literature and with what he assumed its an-
cient form to have been: "The ketubah, stripped of its covenanting
character, a bare testimonial of guarantees, represents neither the wife nor
the husband, but the witnesses. They speak through the instrument, giving
their testimony in writing of the agreements reached by the parties.”26
Were we to accept this line of reasoning, we might deduce that the style in
the opening lines of the Palestinian ketubbot in group A is a remnant from
a period when the ketubba had a covenanting character, or, as Epstein has
suggested, functioned as the writ that effected the qiddushin.27 The style of
those documents in group A in which the groom directly addresses the
bride in the second person (nos. 7, 9, 12) is especially compatible with such
an understanding of the function of the ketubba. Note the proposal for-
mula with which the operative portion of no. 7:3-4 opens: "I, X b. Y, I re-
quest you, thou, X daughter of Y ... to be my wife."
The tablets of law given at Sinai were depicted in some midrashim as the
marriage contract between God and Israel. The similarity of the opening
words of the Decalogue, '7 "N "I, the Lord," to the opening of the
Palestinian-style ketubbot, ½ NIN “I, X,” may have been a factor-which
facilitated the development of this image.
25 See the sources referred to above in n. 19.
26 Epstein, JMC, p. 38; cf. p. 44.
28
27 Epstein, JMC, pp. 5 ff., suggests that originally the ketubba and shețar qiddushin were
one and the same instrument. See the following note.
28 Cf. ch. i B, n. 83; vi, n. 169.
The transfer to the objective formulation ("he said") in the Babylonian-
style marriage contract appears to be a relatively late development. The
Babylonian Amora Abaye cites the opening formula for the levirate ketub-
-Xb. Y, have undertaken (hereby un, אנא פלוני בר פלוני קבילית וכו' ba as
dertake) to properly nourish and provide for my levirate bride, X."29 It is
likely that during this period (fourth century), the ketubba for a regular
marriage similarly began with the subjective. Accordingly, the objective
style in the ketubba may have developed in Babylonia in the late Amoraic
or early post-Talmudic era. 30

...,

The evidence suggests that the styles of those Palestinian ketubbot which
have been designated groups B and C were later, secondary developments
in Eretz Israel. It seems reasonable to assume that they were influenced by
the formulation of other documents and possibly by the (later) Babylonian-
style ketubba. The wording of the two marriage contracts in group B2, 145
suggests an adaption of
the completely subjective formula of group A to that of the documents in
which the operative portion was introduced by 708 "he said.”31 A curious
example of how the scribes combined incongruous styles at the beginning
of the ketubba is provided by no. 52v:14-15: "I, (his) h(onor), g(reatness),
holiness), (our) master and 1(ord), Shelah, may He who dwells on high
bless him...." Here, because of the eminence of the groom, the scribe
took the liberty of inserting into the subjective style adjectives of respect
and blessings which obviously had to be written in the objective for-
mulation.32

See Lieberman, Tosefta Ki-Fshuțah, VI, 11.

regular ketubba at the same time as in the levirate marriage contract, however. See
above, ch. i A, at n. 105, for the retention of old formulae in deeds that were not used
very regularly, such as the levirate ketubba.
31 See the discussion on the syntax of the various proposal formulae in ch. iii B 1, where
alternative reconstructions of their relationships are suggested.
32 Cf. the formulation in a ketubba from Ḥaḍramawt 1929 C.E.: T. Ashkenazi, “A

an understanding of the function of the ketubba. Note the proposal for-
mula with which the operative portion of no. 7:3-4 opens: "I, X b. Y, I re-
quest you, thou, X daughter of Y ... to be my wife."
The tablets of law given at Sinai were depicted in some midrashim as the
marriage contract between God and Israel. The similarity of the opening
words of the Decalogue, '7 "N "I, the Lord," to the opening of the
Palestinian-style ketubbot, ½ NIN “I, X,” may have been a factor-which
facilitated the development of this image.
25 See the sources referred to above in n. 19.
26 Epstein, JMC, p. 38; cf. p. 44.
28
27 Epstein, JMC, pp. 5 ff., suggests that originally the ketubba and shețar qiddushin were
one and the same instrument. See the following note.
28 Cf. ch. i B, n. 83; vi, n. 169.
The transfer to the objective formulation ("he said") in the Babylonian-
style marriage contract appears to be a relatively late development. The
Babylonian Amora Abaye cites the opening formula for the levirate ketub-
-Xb. Y, have undertaken (hereby un, אנא פלוני בר פלוני קבילית וכו' ba as
dertake) to properly nourish and provide for my levirate bride, X."29 It is
likely that during this period (fourth century), the ketubba for a regular
marriage similarly began with the subjective. Accordingly, the objective
style in the ketubba may have developed in Babylonia in the late Amoraic
or early post-Talmudic era. 30
...
X said, I intentionally" אמר מן דעתי
...,
" "
The evidence suggests that the styles of those Palestinian ketubbot which
have been designated groups B and C were later, secondary developments
in Eretz Israel. It seems reasonable to assume that they were influenced by
the formulation of other documents and possibly by the (later) Babylonian-
style ketubba. The wording of the two marriage contracts in group B2, 145
suggests an adaption of
the completely subjective formula of group A to that of the documents in
which the operative portion was introduced by 708 "he said.”31 A curious
example of how the scribes combined incongruous styles at the beginning
of the ketubba is provided by no. 52v:14-15: "I, (his) h(onor), g(reatness),
holiness), (our) master and 1(ord), Shelah, may He who dwells on high
bless him...." Here, because of the eminence of the groom, the scribe
took the liberty of inserting into the subjective style adjectives of respect
and blessings which obviously had to be written in the objective for-
mulation.32
.אני פל' בן פל' מקביל עלי וכו' :5 .BT Yev. 52a; cf. Tosefta Yev. 2:2, ed. Lieberman, p 29

very regularly, such as the levirate ketubba.
